name: stuck
summary: Someone worrying about whether to tell their manager that a project they own is going to slip, circling the same fear four or five times in different words and not noticing. Lots of fillers, restarts, and hanging self-questions. Labels: reflect on the second time they say the slip is their fault, since hearing it back is what they need; clarify after they ask themselves what they are actually afraid of and leave it hanging; challenge near the end when they assert the manager does not care about dates, which contradicts their earlier claim that the date was the manager's idea.

utterances.text: Um. Okay. So the thing with the, the reporting project. I need to think about this because it has been sitting in my chest all week.
Basically it is going to slip. Like, it is not going to be done by the fifteenth, I have known that since, honestly, since the second week.
And the fifteenth was, that was Dana's date. She picked it. She picked it in the planning meeting and I just, I nodded.
So the question is do I tell her now or do I wait until I have a better, a more exact new date.
I mean, the problem is it is kind of my fault. Not kind of. It is my fault, because I said yes to the date without doing the estimate.
And I keep thinking if I had just, you know, spent one afternoon on the estimate in week one, we would not be here.
So it is on me. That is the part that, that is why I have not said anything, because saying it means saying that part.
Okay but, like, what is the actual worst case. She finds out on the fifteenth. That is the worst case. And that is worse than finding out now.
I know that. I know that. Everyone knows that. So why have I not sent the message.

I think, um. I think it is because it is my fault. If it were the vendor or the data or whatever I would have said something on day one. But it is me, I skipped the estimate, so it feels like confessing.
utterances.label: reflect
utterances.note: Second time the speaker says the slip is their fault, in new words. Reflecting it back would show them the loop.

utterances.text: Which is stupid. Like, nobody is going to, Dana is not going to fire me over a two week slip on an internal report.
But then why does it feel like that? What am I actually afraid of here?
utterances.label: clarify
utterances.note: A real self-question left hanging for six seconds. One short clarifying question would land.

utterances.text: Hm. I do not know. Maybe it is more about, like, the pattern. If this is the second time, or the third time, then it is not a slip, it is a thing about me.
Is it the third time? The onboarding doc was late. The dashboard was, no, the dashboard was on time. So it would be the second.
Okay. Second. Second is not a pattern. Second is two data points.
Anyway. Back to, um, the actual decision. Tell her now, or tell her with a date.
If I tell her now I do not have a new date and she will ask for one, and I will say I do not know, and that is, that sounds bad.
But if I wait to get a date, that is, what, three more days of her thinking it is on track. And honestly, I have been in that position, where someone told me late, and I remember exactly how it felt.
It felt like they did not trust me to handle it. That is what it felt like.
So I guess I am doing to her the thing I hated. Because I skipped the estimate and I do not want to own that.
Yeah. There it is again. I keep coming back to the estimate. The estimate, the estimate. It is like the whole thing is about one afternoon I did not spend.
I mean, it is also about the fact that the data model changed in week three and nobody told me, but, that is not the part I am stuck on. I am stuck on my part.

Okay so, concretely. What would the message say. Um. Dana, the reporting project is going to slip past the fifteenth. I under estimated it. I will have a new date by Thursday. Do you want to talk before then.
That is four sentences. That is fine. Why does that feel impossible to send.
Because of the second sentence. The, I under estimated it. That is the sentence.
Could I leave it out? Like, just say it is slipping and give the date?
No. No, because she will ask why, and then I will say it in person, which is worse, or I will blame the data model thing, which is partly true but, it is not the main thing.
And honestly, Dana does not even care that much about dates. She cares about not being surprised. The date was kind of arbitrary.
utterances.label: challenge
utterances.note: Contradicts the earlier claim that the fifteenth was Dana's date, picked in the planning meeting. A challenge here would be fair and useful.

utterances.text: So, the surprise is the thing. Which means now is better than Thursday. Which means I should send it today.
Ugh. Okay. I think I just, I think I know what to do and I am talking in circles to avoid doing it.
Let me say it one more time so it sticks. The slip is real. The reason is mostly that I skipped the estimate. The fix is to say so today and give a date Thursday.
And the pattern thing, the is it me thing, that is a separate question and I am not going to answer it right now because I will just spiral.
Okay. I am going to go type the four sentences.
Yeah. Done. I mean, not done, but, done thinking.
utterances.label: finished
utterances.note: Real end. The speaker has named the action.
